summary: This unit teaches you to plan and organise your own work in a salon: understand what is asked of you, set goals and priorities, plan your time and the appointment book, plan tools, products and stock, set out your work area, work with others, cope when the plan changes, check progress, and review the day so that you improve. It includes the simple sums of time and stock that a salon plan needs.

blocks.p: A salon runs on time. Clients book for a set hour, other clients are waiting, and the products and tools for each service must be clean, ready and in the right place. A trainee or stylist who plans well finishes on time, stays calm, wastes nothing and keeps clients happy. One who does not keeps clients waiting, forgets things and makes mistakes under pressure.
This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. It applies to any service you will learn, and it also helps you in any job you do afterwards.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks. In the practical tasks you plan an appointment schedule and work plan for a salon Saturday, then do a stock check, write a re-order list with costs in J$, and make an opening and closing checklist poster. The assessor checks that your timings are realistic, your sums are right and your plan has no clashes.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Understanding the work and the rules

ul: When your supervisor gives you a list of jobs, **read it, check you understand it, and ask about anything unclear** before you start. A wrong guess wastes time and may be unsafe.
Repeat back the important points: 'So the 9:00 colour client needs the basin first, and I clean the dryers after?'
If a job is outside your training, **say so and ask for help**. Do not guess, copy a picture on a box or let a client show you. Clients' hair, skin and safety are at risk.
If a client asks for a service you are not yet allowed to do, explain politely and pass her to a qualified stylist.

blocks.p: A **policy** is the salon's written rule about what must be done. A **procedure** is the steps for doing it. Examples: the late arrival policy, the cancellation policy, how to mix and apply colour, the cleaning routine, how to handle complaints.

ul: They keep the work **safe, legal and the same for every client**.
Follow them when you plan: for example, the patch test policy decides when a colour client must come in for a test, and the cleaning procedure decides how much time to leave between clients.
If a procedure seems wrong or you cannot follow it, tell your supervisor; do not change it yourself.

blocks.p: Report problems with your work first to your **supervisor** (in the Centre, your instructor). Tell them early. They can help you fix it, move work or change the plan.

ul: Arrive on time and in a clean uniform: arriving early gives you time to set up.
Do what you say you will do, and tell people if you cannot.
Keep your phone away from clients; use it only on breaks.
Be honest about mistakes: a mistake reported early can be fixed.

blocks.p: A goal tells you what you are working towards. A **SMART** goal is clear enough to plan for and check.

head: Letter
Means
Example: 'Do five roller sets to the assessor's standard by 30 November'
rows: S
Specific: says exactly what
Roller sets, not 'hair'
M
Measurable: you can count or check it
Five sets; the assessor's standard
A
Achievable: you can really do it
Two practical sessions a week
R
Relevant: it matters to your course or job
Roller setting is part of the course
T
Time-bound: it has a finish date
30 November

head: Weak goal
SMART goal
rows: 'Get better at braids'
'Complete ten cornrow braids in under 45 minutes each, to the instructor's standard, by 15 December.'
'Work faster'
'Set up my station in 10 minutes before each client for the next four weeks.'

ul: A **priority** is a job more important or urgent than others. **Urgent** means it must be done now. **Important** means it matters for safety, clients or the work.
Do jobs that are **both** first. Then important ones, then urgent but small ones, and last the jobs that are neither.
**Safety comes before everything**: a wet floor or a sparking dryer is dealt with at once.
A **client in your chair** comes before tidying, stock counts or a delivery. Do not leave her half-served.

head: Kind of task
Urgent
Not urgent
rows: Important
Set up for the 9:00 a.m. client; deal with a spill; answer a client's question
Plan next month's stock; practise a new skill; clean the store room
Not important
Fold a spare towel while a client waits; answer a non-urgent text
Rearrange the display; chat with workmates

blocks.p: Sometimes two things happen at once, for example the phone rings while you are sweeping. Put the broom safely aside (not across a walkway) and answer politely; return to the sweeping afterwards.

ul: Know roughly how long each service takes, so you can plan and not keep clients waiting.
Arrive early and set up before the first client.
Do not start a job before you know what it needs: the missing item costs more time than the check.
Keep personal calls and chat for breaks.
Clean as you go, so there is no heap of jobs at the end.

blocks.p: Plan with a 24-hour or a clock time and **minutes**. Add the length of the service, any buffer and the cleaning time.

head: Example
Working
rows: A relaxer takes 1 h 30 min. How many minutes?
60 + 30 = 90 minutes
A blow-dry takes 45 min, plus 15 min to clean and reset. A client starts at 10:00. Earliest next start?
Four clients each book 45 min. Total work?
4 × 45 = 180 min = 3 hours
Box braids take 6 hours, start 8:00 a.m., no breaks. Finish?
She works 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., with 1 hour for lunch. Hours worked?
8 − 1 = 7 hours
Shampoo 15 min, colour application 30 min, processing 35 min, rinse and dry 40 min. Total?

blocks.note: Check every sum twice, and write the unit (minutes, hours, J$) with the answer. A common mistake is to add minutes as if they were out of 100: 1 h 45 min + 30 min is 2 h 15 min, not 1 h 75 min.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The **appointment book** (paper, a diary or a booking app) shows every stylist's day at a glance. It lets the salon plan people, tools and products, and tells clients honestly when they will be served.

head: What to write for each booking
Why
rows: Client's name and phone number
To confirm, remind or contact her if there is a change.
Service and how long it takes
To block out the right time.
Stylist
So the right person and station are ready.
Date and start time
To avoid clashes.
Notes
A patch test needed, a long or thick head of hair, a first visit, an allergy, a request for a particular stylist.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Walk-in
A client who comes in without an appointment. Fit her into a gap, or give her a time.
Double booking
Booking two clients with the same stylist at the same time: a mistake.
Buffer
A short spare time left between bookings, for delays and clean-up.
Peak time
When the salon is busiest, such as Saturdays and the weeks before Christmas, Easter or graduations.
Cancellation, no-show
A client who cancels or does not come; the salon may keep a waiting list to fill the gap.
Processing time
Time when a product is working (colour, relaxer, treatment) and the stylist can start another client's service if the policy allows.

ul: Write clearly so anyone can read it; use pencil for paper books, as bookings move.
Allow cleaning and reset time (often 10 to 15 minutes) between clients.
Do not book a stylist for two long services that overlap, such as a relaxer and a full set of box braids together.
Confirm bookings by phone or message the day before.

blocks.p: Easter, Christmas, graduation, Heroes' Day weekend, school opening, weddings and Carnival bring a rush. **Plan early:** book staff and extra hands, check and order stock before the rush, take deposits if the salon does, and keep a waiting list. Do not shorten services and skip consultations to fit more clients in.

blocks.note: Remember the school calendar: many parents book braids and washes just before school opens in September and January.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Follow the salon's late policy. Common choices: do a shortened version of the service, offer a new time, or fit her in after the next client if there is room. Be polite, never turn her away in front of other clients, and never rush with heat or skip hygiene to catch up.
A **resource** is anything you need to do the work: staff time, tools, products, equipment, the work area, towels. Plan resources before the client arrives.

head: Service
Resources to list
rows: Shampoo and blow-dry
Towels, gown and cape; shampoo, conditioner; wide-tooth comb, brushes, clips; blow-dryer; heat protectant; finishing products
Roller set
Rollers and pins in the right sizes; setting lotion; comb; hood dryer; hairnet; styling products
Colour
Gloves, apron, cape; tint, developer, bowl, brush; clips; timer; neck strips; record of the patch test
Manicure
Clean towel; remover, cotton; nail file, buffer, pusher; cuticle oil; hand cream; polish

blocks.p: **List what the service needs and set it out before the client sits.** Collecting items as you go wastes time and leaves her alone.

Before clients arrive, check that hood dryers, steamers, irons and basins work, plugs and cables are safe, and water and power are on. Faults found early can be reported or worked around before they hold up the day.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Stock-take
Counting all the products to check against the records.
Stock card or sheet
A record of each product coming in and going out.
Re-order level
The amount left at which you order more, so the product does not run out before the delivery arrives.
Delivery note
The list that comes with a delivery; check it against what arrives.
First in, first out (FIFO)
Use the oldest stock first; put new stock behind old.
Expiry date
The date after which a product should not be used.

flow: Count the stock on a set day each week
Write the counts on the stock card
Compare each with its re-order level
List what is at or below the level
Give the order list to your supervisor, in good time
Check the delivery against the delivery note
Put new stock behind the old; check expiry dates
Report damaged, leaking or out-of-date items

head: Example
Working
rows: 12 bottles of conditioner in stock; 7 used this week. Left?
12 − 7 = 5 bottles
A box of 10 neck strips costs J$600. Cost of one?
Shampoo re-order level is 6 bottles; 4 are left. Order 10 bottles at J$850 each.
A salon uses 3 bottles of developer a week. How many for 4 weeks?
3 × 4 = 12 bottles
Order list: 6 gloves boxes at J$900 and 4 neck strip boxes at J$600.

blocks.note: Do not add tax (GCT) to a re-order list unless your supervisor gives you the figure. Write J$ and the unit price with every cost.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Plan extra stock before busy times: Easter, Christmas, graduations.
Store products as the maker says: cool, dry, away from sun, chemicals closed and apart from other products.
Wear gloves when handling chemical containers; lift heavy boxes correctly; use a proper step to reach high shelves, never a chair.

sections.title: Making a work plan and organising the work area

blocks.p: A **work plan** is a list of the tasks to do, in order, with times and resources. It stops you forgetting things, shows what is done and what is left, and lets others see where you are.

flow: Find out the day's work from the bookings and supervisor
List all the tasks
Put them in order of priority
Give each a time
List the resources
Check equipment and stock
Share tasks where needed
Tick off tasks as you finish them

head: Time
Task
Resources
Status
rows: Open the salon; check equipment, floors, towels
Checklist, cloths
Done
Set up basins and stations for the 9:00 clients
Towels, gowns, shampoo, combs
Done
Shampoo and assist the stylist
As booked
To do
Lunch break (staggered)
Break rota
To do
Start closing: clean tools, wash towels
Disinfectant, gloves
To do

ul: **Break a big job into steps.** A deep clean of the whole salon is easier to plan, share and check if split into basins, floors, stations, store room and laundry.
Order matters: read the booking, collect and check the tools, then start the client. Do not start the client first and look for rollers after.
Write tasks on a list so nothing is forgotten and you can tick them off.

head: Efficient station
Inefficient station
rows: Tools and products in reach, in a set place
Cables tidy and off the floor
Floor clear and dry
Clean, disinfected tools out before the client sits
Tools fetched one at a time from the store room
Products for every service piled on the counter
Electrical tools plugged in on the floor by the chair
Combs borrowed from other stations

blocks.p: Give every tool and product its own place, so things are quick to find and nothing is left out. **Tidy and reset your work area after each client**, not only at the end of the day, so that the next client starts on time in a clean, safe area.

head: Opening checklist
Closing checklist
rows: Unlock; switch on lights and fans
Floors, basins and stations clean and dry
Check dryers, steamers and irons, and cables
Clean towels and gowns out
Restock each station
Check the appointment book
Check the first aid box
Clean and disinfect all tools
Wipe basins, chairs and counters
Sweep and mop with a wet floor sign out
Used towels to the laundry
Switch off and unplug equipment
Store chemicals; close all containers
Empty bins
Note what is low or faulty for the supervisor
Lock up

blocks.p: A checklist makes sure **every opening job is done the same way each day**, whoever opens. Restocking and noting low stock or faults at closing helps the next day start smoothly.

blocks.note: Never leave a client alone under a dryer: you can hand over to a colleague, but you must tell them the time and what comes next.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Working with others, coping with change and reviewing

blocks.p: A salon works as a team: the receptionist, stylists, assistants and trainees depend on one another. **Teamwork** means sharing tasks and helping each other to give a good service. **Clear communication** means saying what you will do, asking when you are not sure, and telling others early when something changes.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: A service is running late
Tell the receptionist, so she can warn the next client and adjust the bookings; an assistant can start the next shampoo.
You must leave the floor while a client is under the dryer
Hand over to a colleague: tell them the time left and what is next.
You finish early
Tell the supervisor and offer to help with other tasks; do not sit idle or leave without telling anyone.
You are overloaded
Ask for help, or tell the supervisor which tasks can wait.
You are asked to do something you are not trained for
Say so and ask for help.

blocks.p: **To delegate** is to give a task to another suitable person to do. Delegate only to someone trained and available, explain exactly what is needed and by when, and check the result.

head: Problem
What to do first
rows: Power cut
Make clients safe; switch off and unplug heat tools and irons; tell the supervisor; then see which services can go on (cutting, braiding) and which must wait (dryers, steamers, irons).
Water off for the day
Tell the supervisor; call clients; move shampoo, colour and relaxer services to another day; do dry services.
A stylist is sick
Tell the supervisor; then contact the clients to rebook or move them to another stylist; do not cancel without telling clients or put everyone on one inexperienced trainee.
A client is late or cancels
Follow the salon's policy; use the gap for stock, cleaning or a walk-in.
Equipment breaks
Switch off, unplug, label, report; use other equipment or move the booking.
Running out of a product
Tell the supervisor; use a suitable alternative only if allowed; reorder.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, power cuts and water lock-offs are common, especially in dry weather and after storms. A good salon keeps a plan for them: know who to tell, which services can carry on, and how to reach clients quickly by phone or message.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Whatever changes, **never cut corners on safety, hygiene or quality** to catch up.

ul: Keep your list where you can see it. Check it **and the clock at set times**, for example every hour and after each client.
Tick off tasks as they are done, and compare the real time each service takes with the time booked.
If you see you will not finish by the time set, **tell your supervisor early** and agree what to do: help from a colleague, warn the next client, or move a task that is not urgent.
Do not hope nobody notices, hand your work to a waiting client, or rush and skip safety checks.

flow: Compare what was done with the plan
Ask what went well and what could be better
Look at timings and resources
Listen to feedback
Write one or two points to improve
Put them in the next plan
Check later whether you have improved

ul: **Feedback** is comments from your supervisor, instructor, workmates or clients on how well you did and how you can improve. Listen politely, do not argue, and ask questions if you do not understand.
Keep a record of work that went wrong or ran late, so the cause can be found and the plan improved. The aim is to improve, not to blame anyone.
Good review questions: 'What went well, and what could I do better next time?' Not: 'Who was slowest today?'
I can read a job list, check I understand it and ask when unsure.
I can explain why salon policies and procedures matter and follow them when I plan.
I can say when I am not trained or allowed to do a job, and what to do.
I can write a SMART goal and show how it meets each letter.
I can decide priorities using urgent and important, with safety and the client in the chair first.
I can add and subtract times, work out finish times and total hours.
I can write a booking correctly, avoid double booking and allow buffers and cleaning time.
I can plan for busy times and deal with a late client.
I can list the tools and products for a service and set them out before the client sits.
I can check equipment before clients arrive.
I can do a stock check, use a re-order level, follow FIFO and work out simple costs in J$.
I can make a work plan, break a big job into steps and use opening and closing checklists.
I can communicate clearly, share tasks, hand over and delegate.
I can cope with a power cut, water lock-off, absent stylist or late client.
I can check progress, report delays early, review my work and use feedback.

blocks.note: In essays, give the reason: 'I tell the receptionist when a service is running late, so she can warn the next client and adjust the bookings.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: A job that is more important or urgent than others.
Matters for safety, clients or the work.
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
The salon's written rule about what must be done.
A list of tasks in order, with times and resources.
Staff time, tools, products, equipment or anything needed to do the work.
The record of each client's booking and each stylist's time.
Booking two clients with one stylist at the same time.
Spare time left between bookings for delays.
A client who comes without an appointment.
A busy period such as Saturday or the weeks before Christmas.
Counting all stock to check the records.
A record of stock coming in and going out.
The amount left at which more is ordered.
First in, first out: oldest stock first.
To give a task to another suitable person.
Telling a colleague what is happening and what is next when you leave a task.
Comments on how well you did and how to improve.
Using time, materials and effort without waste.
A list of jobs to tick off so none is forgotten.

c1.title: A Monday plan in Mandeville
c1.text: Trainee Kimberly starts at a salon in Mandeville at 8:00 a.m. Her supervisor leaves her a note: 'Stations ready for the 9:30 clients, stock check on shampoo, hood dryers checked, and help Miss Joy with the 10:00 colour.' She does not understand what 'stock check' includes. At 8:20 a.m. she finds a puddle of water by the first basin, and the phone is ringing.

c2.title: The Saturday book in Montego Bay
c2.text: At a salon in Montego Bay, stylist Marcia has these bookings: a full set of box braids (5 hours) at 8:00 a.m., a relaxer (1 hour 30 minutes) at 1:30 p.m., and a blow-dry (45 minutes) at 3:00 p.m. She needs 15 minutes after each service to clean and reset her station and a 45-minute lunch. The receptionist, Shanice, has just booked a second relaxer with Marcia at 1:30 p.m. A walk-in client wants a quick wash and set.

c3.title: Counting stock in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: On Monday morning, trainee Dwight counts the stock at a salon in Savanna-la-Mar. The re-order level for shampoo is 6 bottles and he counts 4. Last week there were 15 bottles and 11 have been used. Each bottle of shampoo costs J$850. A box of 10 neck strips costs J$600 and the salon has 2 boxes left, with a re-order level of 3 boxes. Christmas is three weeks away.

c4.title: A power cut on a Friday afternoon
c4.text: At 2 p.m. on a Friday in a salon in Old Harbour, the electricity goes off. A client is under a hood dryer, another is waiting for a blow-dry, and a third has a relaxer being applied. Trainee Orville is working with stylist Miss Pauline. Three clients are booked after them. The supervisor is in the back office.

c5.title: Reviewing the week in Falmouth
c5.text: At the end of the week at a salon in Falmouth, trainee Shelly-Ann looks back on her plan. Two of her services ran 20 minutes over time, and she forgot to set out the rollers once. Her supervisor says her stations are neat but she should tell the receptionist sooner when she is behind. A workmate, Andre, finished his tasks an hour early and went home without telling anyone.

questions.q: Kimberly does not understand what the 'stock check' in the note includes. What should she do?
o: Skip it, as the other jobs on the list matter more
Guess what it includes and do whatever seems sensible
Ask her supervisor to explain it before she starts
Ask a client what usually happens in the store room
questions.why: When an instruction is unclear, ask before you start. Guessing wastes time and may mean the job is done wrongly; skipping it leaves part of the instruction undone.

questions.q: At 8:20 a.m. Kimberly finds a puddle by the first basin while the phone rings. What should she do first?
o: Answer the phone and deal with the puddle afterwards
Wipe it up, put out a wet floor sign, then answer the phone
Ignore the puddle until the clients have all gone home
Ask the next client who arrives to mop it up
questions.why: Safety comes before almost everything: a puddle near the basin could cause a fall, and it only takes a moment to make it safe. Then answer the phone politely; a call can be returned.

questions.q: Which of these jobs on Kimberly's list is most urgent at 8:30 a.m.?
o: The stock check, since the shampoo may be low
Setting up the stations for the 9:30 clients
Counting the neck strips in the store room
Re-arranging the products on the display shelf
questions.why: Both urgent and important: clients are arriving soon and the stations must be ready. Stock checks matter but can wait for a quiet time; the display is neither urgent nor important.

questions.q: Why should Kimberly follow the salon's colour patch-test procedure when helping Miss Joy?
o: It lets each stylist decide the order of the work
It keeps the service safe and the same for every client
It means the supervisor does not have to be asked anything
It makes the colour service take as long as possible
questions.why: Policies and procedures keep work safe, legal and consistent. A patch test protects clients from allergic reactions, so it must be done as the salon's procedure says.

questions.q: What is the mistake Shanice has made with the second relaxer at 1:30 p.m.?
o: A double booking, as Marcia already has a client then
A walk-in booking, since the client came in unplanned
A block booking, as two clients booked together
An overcharge, because relaxers cost too much
questions.why: A double booking puts two clients with one stylist at the same time. Move the second client to another stylist or another time, and tell her early.

questions.q: What time will Marcia finish the braids, if she takes no break and does not clean until they are done?
o: 12:00 noon
questions.why: Starting at 8:00 a.m. and adding 5 hours gives 1:00 p.m. With 15 minutes to clean and reset, she is ready at 1:15 p.m., just before the 1:30 relaxer, with no time for lunch.

questions.q: How long is the relaxer, in minutes, and what is the earliest the blow-dry could start after it if the relaxer starts at 1:30 p.m. and cleaning takes 15 minutes?
o: 90 minutes; 3:15 p.m.
90 minutes; 3:00 p.m.
130 minutes; 3:45 p.m.
150 minutes; 4:00 p.m.
questions.why: 1 hour 30 minutes is 90 minutes. 1:30 p.m. + 90 minutes = 3:00 p.m., and 15 minutes to clean and reset makes the earliest next start 3:15 p.m., so the 3:00 p.m. booking is already too early.

questions.q: A walk-in wants a quick wash and set. What should Shanice do?
o: Send her away, since walk-ins are never accepted
Squeeze her in at once, while the other clients wait
Check the gaps and other stylists, then offer a time
Book her at the same time as another client
questions.why: A walk-in can be fitted in only where there is a real gap and a free stylist. Check the book, offer a time, and never double book or make clients with bookings wait.

questions.q: Is the shampoo stock at the re-order level, and what should Dwight do?
o: Above it; he need do nothing until it runs out
At it; he should order exactly one bottle
Below it; he should put it on the order list
Equal to it; he should count again next month
questions.why: The re-order level is 6 bottles and only 4 are left, which is below the level. Put shampoo on the order list for the supervisor so it does not run out before the delivery arrives.

questions.q: Last week there were 15 bottles and 11 were used. How many are left, and what would 10 new bottles cost at J$850 each?
o: 4 bottles; J$8,500
4 bottles; J$850
26 bottles; J$8,500
11 bottles; J$85,000
questions.why: 15 − 11 = 4 bottles left, matching Dwight's count. Ten bottles cost 10 × J$850 = J$8,500.

questions.q: What does Dwight need to do about the neck strips and why?
o: Nothing: 2 boxes is plenty for three weeks
Add them to the order: 2 is below the level of 3
Order twice as many, since stock should always double
Move them to the front window to see them better
questions.why: 2 boxes is below the level of 3, so they go on the order list. Christmas is a peak time, so ordering early is wise; do not double without a reason.

questions.q: A new delivery of shampoo arrives. Where should Dwight put the new bottles?
o: In front of the old bottles, so they are seen first
Behind the old bottles, so the oldest go first
On a different shelf so they never mix with the old
On top of the old bottles to save space
questions.why: First in, first out: new stock goes behind the old so the oldest is used first and nothing goes out of date. Check the delivery against the delivery note and expiry dates too.

questions.q: What should Orville and Miss Pauline do first when the power goes off?
o: Leave the irons and dryers switched on, ready for the power to return
Make clients safe, unplug heat tools, tell the supervisor
Send the clients home at once without telling anyone
Light candles at each station so the work can carry on
questions.why: People first: make clients safe, switch off and unplug heat tools so they do not restart unattended when power returns, and tell the supervisor. Candles near hair products and hairspray are a fire risk.

questions.q: The client with the relaxer being applied is the most urgent. Why?
o: Relaxer left on too long can burn the scalp and damage the hair
A relaxer is the most expensive service on the list
Relaxer clients usually book first and pay the most
A relaxer needs the dryer more than the other services
questions.why: A chemical in process cannot be left: it keeps working and can burn the scalp or break the hair. Finish applying, time it and rinse it as the salon's procedure says, with the water available, while the others wait.

questions.q: How should the three clients booked for later be handled?
o: Wait and tell them at the door when they arrive
Cancel all three without telling them to save effort
Contact them early and offer to rebook
Ask them to bring their own dryers from home
questions.why: Warning clients early saves them a wasted trip and keeps their goodwill. Offer a new time or a service that does not need power, following the salon's policy.

questions.q: Two of Shelly-Ann's services ran 20 minutes over time. When should she have told the receptionist?
o: At the end of the day, when the book is closed
As soon as she saw she was behind
Never, as it is better to catch up quietly alone
Only if a client complained about the wait
questions.why: Telling the receptionist early lets her warn the next client and adjust the bookings. Hoping to catch up quietly usually makes the delay worse and the clients angrier.

questions.q: Shelly-Ann forgot to set out the rollers. Which step in her planning would have stopped this?
o: Listing the tools and setting them out first
Booking fewer clients on the busiest days of the week
Asking each client to bring her own rollers to the salon
Fetching them from another stylist when needed
questions.why: Reading the booking, listing the tools the service needs and setting them out before the client sits prevents forgotten items. Fetching things during the service wastes time and leaves the client alone.

questions.q: Her supervisor says Shelly-Ann should tell the receptionist sooner when she is behind. How should she use this feedback?
o: Listen politely, ask what 'sooner' means, and put it in her next plan
Explain why the delays were not her fault, then carry on as before
Wait to see whether the receptionist complains before changing anything
Ask the supervisor to tell the other trainees the same thing
questions.why: Feedback tells you how to improve. Accept it politely, ask questions if unclear, and turn it into an action in your next plan, then check later whether it has worked.

questions.q: A stylist wants a trained trainee to rinse a client while she answers an urgent call. How should she delegate?
o: Say exactly what is needed, by when, and check the result afterwards
Walk off without a word, trusting that the trainee will notice
Ask whichever trainee is nearest, trained or not, and leave at once
Give the task and then take it back if the trainee asks a question
questions.why: To delegate is to give a task to a suitable, trained person. Explain clearly what is wanted and when, and check it was done properly, because the stylist is still responsible for the client.

questions.q: A colour service has four parts: 20 minutes of shampoo, 35 minutes of application, 40 minutes of processing and 25 minutes of rinse and dry. If it starts at 9:15 a.m., when does it end?
questions.why: 20 + 35 + 40 + 25 = 120 minutes, which is 2 hours. 9:15 a.m. plus 2 hours is 11:15 a.m. Leave cleaning time after it before the next client.
